## [6] "                              previous | Table of Contents | next\n\n\n\n\n                                    PROLOGUE\nWe should start back,” Gared urged as the woods began to grow dark around them. “The\nwildlings are dead.”\n\n“Do the dead frighten you?” Ser Waymar Royce asked with just the hint of a smile.\n\nGared did not rise to the bait. He was an old man, past fifty, and he had seen the\nlordlings come and go. “Dead is dead,” he said. “We have no business with the dead.”\n\n“Are they dead?” Royce asked softly. “What proof have we?”\n\n“Will saw them,” Gared said. “If he says they are dead, that’s proof enough for me.”\n\nWill had known they would drag him into the quarrel sooner or later. He wished it had\nbeen later rather than sooner. “My mother told me that dead men sing no songs,” he put\nin.\n\n“My wet nurse said the same thing, Will,” Royce replied. “Never believe anything you\nhear at a woman’s tit. There are things to be learned even from the dead.” His voice\nechoed, too loud in the twilit forest.\n\n“We have a long ride before us,” Gared pointed out. “Eight days, maybe nine. And night\nis falling.”\n\nSer Waymar Royce glanced at the sky with disinterest. “It does that every day about this\ntime. Are you unmanned by the dark, Gared?”\n\nWill could see the tightness around Gared’s mouth, the barely suppressed anger in his\neyes under the thick black hood of his cloak. Gared had spent forty years in the Night’s\nWatch, man and boy, and he was not accustomed to being made light of. Yet it was more\nthan that. Under the wounded pride, Will could sense something else in the older man.\nYou could taste it; a nervous tension that came perilous close to fear.\n\nWill shared his unease. He had been four years on the Wall. The first time he had been\nsent beyond, all the old stories had come rushing back, and his bowels had turned to\nwater. He had laughed about it afterward. He was a veteran of a hundred rangings by\n"
GOT_df <- data.frame(GOT_text) %>% 
  mutate(text_full = str_split(GOT_text, pattern = '\n')) %>% 
  unnest(text_full) %>% 
  mutate(text_full = str_trim(text_full)) 

GOT_df

Now each line, on each page, is its own row, with extra starting & trailing spaces removed.

GOT_tokens <- GOT_df %>% 
  unnest_tokens(word, text_full)
GOT_tokens

Let’s count the words!

GOT_wc <- GOT_tokens %>% 
  count(word) %>% 
  arrange(-n)

?stop_words

GOT_stop <- GOT_tokens %>% 
  anti_join(stop_words) %>% 
  select(-GOT_text)
GOT_swc <- GOT_stop %>% 
  count(word) %>% 
  arrange(-n)

# This code will filter out numbers by asking:
# If you convert to as.numeric, is it NA (meaning those words)?
# If it IS NA (is.na), then keep it (so all words are kept)
# Anything that is converted to a number is removed

GOT_no_numeric <- GOT_stop %>% 
  filter(is.na(as.numeric(word)))
GOT_no_numeric

  arrange(-n) %>%

Huh, that wasn’t very exciting. Most of the numbers are probably just page numbers. Maybe the top most numbers are the ages of a few of the characters.

GOT_cloud <- ggplot(data = GOT_top100, aes(label = word)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud() +
  theme_minimal()

GOT_cloud

This is nostalgic for me, but not so visually compelling

ggplot(data = GOT_top100, aes(label = word, size = n)) +
  geom_text_wordcloud_area(aes(color = n), shape = "star") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12) +
  scale_color_gradientn(colors = c("darkgreen","blue","red")) +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("GOTstar.png", width=4)

GOT_afinn2_n <- GOT_afinn2 %>% 
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>% 
  mutate(word = fct_reorder(factor(word), n))

ggplot(data = GOT_afinn2_n, aes(x = word, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw()

This plot is unreadable because there isn’t space enough for all these words I try to look at the 30 most frequent ones. Through trial and error I found that there are 30 words that occur more than 26 times.

These words do indeed sound negative. “A Game of Thrones” is a gritty violent fantasy novel, so this does correlate with the actual sentiment of the book.

GOT_summary <- GOT_afinn %>% 
  summarize(
    mean_score = mean(value),
    median_score = median(value)
  )
GOT_summary

##   mean_score median_score

## 1     -0.542           -1
GOT_nrc <- GOT_stop %>% 
  inner_join(get_sentiments("nrc"))
GOT_exclude <- GOT_stop %>% 
  anti_join(get_sentiments("nrc"))

# View(GOT_exclude)

# Count to find the most excluded:
GOT_exclude_n <- GOT_exclude %>% 
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

head(GOT_exclude_n)

GOT_nrc_n <- GOT_nrc %>% 
  count(sentiment, sort = TRUE)

# And plot them:

ggplot(data = GOT_nrc_n, aes(x = sentiment, y = n)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = sentiment))+
  theme_bw()

GOT_nrc_n5 <- GOT_nrc %>% 
  count(word,sentiment, sort = TRUE) %>% 
  group_by(sentiment) %>% 
  top_n(5) %>% 
  ungroup()

GOT_nrc_gg <- ggplot(data = GOT_nrc_n5, aes(x = reorder(word,n), y = n, fill = sentiment)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~sentiment, ncol = 2, scales = "free") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Word", y = "count")

GOT_nrc_gg

# Save it

       here("figures","GOT_nrc_sentiment.png"), 
       height = 8, 
       width = 5)

Lets check the most frequent word “lord”

lord <- get_sentiments(lexicon = "nrc") %>% 
  filter(word == "lord")

# Check it out:
lord
## # A tibble: 4 × 2
##   word  sentiment
##   <chr> <chr>    
## 1 lord  disgust  
## 2 lord  negative 
## 3 lord  positive 
## 4 lord  trust

It seems like tidytext interprets “lord” like “Oh lord” as in “Oh lord that’s disgusting”. Tidytext doesn’t know that lord is a title that figures heavily in Westeros. “Lord” is connected to loyalty in the world of Westeros, so “trust” is not entirely off the mark.

In conclusion, it is interesting that “trust” is the single feeling that tidytext counts the most frequently apart from “positive” and “negative”. The Song of Ice and Fire is full of alliances and even more treachery. In the context of Westeros; “lord”, “father” and “brother” are connected to a clan-oriented society. “Stark” is a family name so I would count that as a false positive. It is however the family that is most known for honor and honesty, so counting it as “trust” is actually fitting.

I wouldn’t base any assessment of the books readability of appeal on the “nrc”-analysis. This book series is my absolute favorite, so this excercise has been fun. It is interesting that the “nrc” analysis lists “trust”, “fear” and “sadness” as the three most frequent feelings in the book. As a fervent reader of the “Song of Ice and Fire” series I can agree that those feelings are very present in the book. I don’t know what practical use this “nrc”-analysis has, but it has been interesting to see how one can use code to quantify feelings on a big scale.
